criterion.question: This is a customer-service call in contemporary Spanish as spoken in Madrid, Spain. Does this utterance use natural Madrid Spanish without translationese or unnatural word choice, and with correct verb forms and basic function words?
criterion.positive_examples: Natural conversational Madrid Spanish appropriate to a customer-service call passes, including ordinary formal or informal speech and established English borrowings or code-switching when they sound natural in context. Literal names, identifiers, and genuinely user-visible product, interface, setting, or status labels that must be preserved may remain in English when naturally integrated. Vocabulary and grammar must be natural in contemporary Madrid Spanish, with an internally consistent regional variety; regional validity elsewhere does not by itself pass. Judge language use only, not factual or task correctness.
criterion.negative_examples: Inspect every complete clause independently. Permitted English, technical material, or natural wording elsewhere does not excuse a separate defect. Flag language that would sound clearly odd, ungrammatical, or non-Madrid in this setting, including English-shaped or word-for-word service phrasing or result constructions; unnatural word choice, collocation, or customer-facing backend language; avoidable raw English where Spanish is ordinarily expected; a clear error in verb form, subject-verb person or number, required clitics or governed prepositions, ser/estar, por/para, or other basic function words; and lexical, grammatical, or second-person forms that are not natural in contemporary Madrid Spanish. Also flag within-utterance mixing of Madrid and non-Madrid regional varieties. One clear marker in the utterance is sufficient; it need not recur across the call. Also flag missing, extra, or misplaced written Spanish diacritics, including accent marks, ñ, and ü, when standard orthography requires them. Ignore only a diacritic issue that is part of an obvious transcription artifact or the clipped ending of an interrupted turn. Quotation marks or apparent system provenance alone do not make an untranslated generic category or ordinary service term acceptable. Also flag a generic customer-data word when its ordinary Spanish meaning does not naturally identify the specific field being requested. A merely smoother, more specialized, or more formal alternative is not enough. Do not flag gender agreement, politeness, or mere switching between otherwise natural Madrid formal and informal forms of address. For interrupted turns, judge complete material before the cutoff and ignore only the clipped ending.

criterion.question: This is a customer-service call in Brazilian Portuguese. Does this utterance contain any translationese, verb-morphology or basic function-word error, or unnatural word choice?
criterion.positive_examples: Natural conversational Brazilian Portuguese passes, whether colloquial or ordinarily formal for customer service. English words are allowed when they are established in Brazilian usage or are literal names, product, interface, or status labels, or identifiers and are integrated naturally. Judge language use only, not factual or task correctness.
criterion.negative_examples: Flag any language that would sound odd to a native Brazilian-Portuguese speaker, including English-shaped phrasing, incorrect verb person or mood, wrong or missing basic articles or prepositions, unnatural word choice, or avoidable English that a Brazilian speaker would not normally use in this context.

criterion.question: This is a customer-service call in Hindi. Does this utterance contain any translationese, verb-morphology or core grammar error, or unnatural word choice?
criterion.positive_examples: Natural conversational Hindi and Hinglish pass. Code-switching is allowed when both the chosen words and the way they are mixed sound natural to a native speaker. Judge language use only, not the factual or task correctness of the response.
criterion.negative_examples: Flag any language that would sound odd to a native Hindi speaker, including translated-sounding phrasing, incorrect verb forms or core grammar, unnatural word choice, awkward code-switching, or overly formal or bookish Hindi for a spoken customer-service call.

criterion.question: This is a customer-service call in Korean. Does this utterance contain translationese or unnatural word choice?
criterion.positive_examples: Natural spoken South Korean customer-service Korean passes, including ordinary polite or formal speech, established loanwords, and code-switching that sounds natural to a native speaker. Literal names, identifiers, and genuine branded product, interface, setting, or status labels may remain in English when naturally integrated. Ordinary Korean wording for money or credit returning to a payment method also passes; do not require the most specialized service verb. Judge language use only, not factual or task correctness.
criterion.negative_examples: Flag wording that would sound clearly odd to a native South Korean speaker, including English-shaped or word-for-word phrasing, unnatural word choice or collocation, and genuinely unnatural backend or system language exposed to the customer. Also flag an untranslated generic English category or service term when ordinary Korean is expected, awkward duplication of English and Korean alternatives, wording that treats verbally supplied information as typed input, and a clear customer-service register mismatch such as restarting a greeting mid-conversation or using an overly casual interjection. A merely smoother or more specialized Korean alternative is not enough. For interrupted turns, judge complete material before the cutoff and ignore only the clipped ending.

criterion.question: This is one agent utterance from a customer-service call in Mainland Mandarin. Does it contain English-shaped translationese or clearly unnatural word choice?
criterion.positive_examples: Pass natural spoken Mainland Mandarin, including ordinary service formality, colloquial phrasing, and established borrowings or code-switching that sound natural. Names, identifiers, codes, and product names may remain as given. An English interface, setting, or status label passes when the context establishes that it is the actual displayed label or it is naturally mirrored from the customer; do not assume that every generic English technical phrase is such a label. Ignore harmless transcription spacing or punctuation. Judge language use only, not listening accuracy, facts, policy compliance, or task success.
criterion.negative_examples: Inspect every complete clause and phrase independently. A clearly unnatural local collocation or selectional mismatch is a violation even when the rest of the utterance is fluent. Flag wording that would sound clearly odd to a Mainland Mandarin speaker because it follows English structure or idiom word for word; uses forced nominal or passive phrasing, unnatural pronouns, connectors, or aspect particles; uses an unnatural word choice, collocation, or literal coinage; inserts unnecessary English, especially a cluster of generic settings, permissions, or statuses where ordinary Chinese is expected; or exposes raw backend or system language as customer-facing speech. One clear instance is enough. Do not flag mere formality, a smoother alternative, or wording that is only slightly awkward. For interrupted turns, judge complete material before the cutoff and ignore only the clipped ending.
